# SE-3 completion — generated by `complete.py`, not hand-edited

## 1. The four unmodelled effects, priced

MODEL_VALIDITY §2 lists four things the twin does not model and states that **every one of them biases throughput upward**. That is an admission that every number the twin produces is an upper bound — and an upper bound of unknown size is not usable for an investment decision. Here is the size.

| stage | throughput (parts/h) | factor |
|---|---|---|
| twin as built | 40.0 | — |
| after product mix | 32.5 | 0.813 |
| after changeovers | 18.4 | 0.565 |
| after operators | 17.5 | 0.951 |
| after quality loop | 16.5 | 0.942 |

**The twin overstates throughput by 2.43× (40.0 → 16.5 parts/h.)**

*multiplicative and therefore approximate; the effects interact, mostly in the bad direction -- a changeover during an operator shortage costs more than either alone, because the setup needs the operator who is not there.*

### Product mix moves the bottleneck

| product | bottleneck station | capacity/h |
|---|---|---|
| A | S3 | 43.8 |
| B | S6 | 64.6 |
| C | S4 | 49.0 |

**The bottleneck is not the same station for every product** — stations [3, 4, 6] each take the constraint depending on what is running. A line balanced for the average is balanced for a product it never makes, and the buffer sized for the average bottleneck sits in the wrong place for most of the schedule.

### Changeovers make batch size a throughput decision

| batch | changeovers | setup as share of horizon | throughput/h | WIP |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 5 | 63 | 182.7% | 0.0 | 5 |
| 10 | 31 | 92.2% | 4.8 | 10 |
| 20 | 15 | 43.5% | 35.1 | 20 |
| 40 | 7 | 22.6% | 48.0 | 40 |
| 80 | 3 | 8.7% | 56.7 | 80 |
| 160 | 1 | 5.2% | 58.8 | 160 |

Demand is scaled to what the line can actually make in the horizon (320 parts, 106 per product), and the batch chosen is **20** — the smallest that keeps setup under half the horizon. The first version of this asked for 600 parts against a horizon good for ~320 and reported a setup share of 347%, which is the tell that the scenario was wrong rather than the model.

The matrix is **asymmetric on purpose** — e.g. A->A 0s, A->B 1496s, A->C 1500s — because one direction needs a purge and the other does not. A symmetric matrix makes the sequencing problem trivial and removes the only interesting thing about it.

**This sweep is biased toward large batches** and says so: it models the changeover cost and not the WIP cost, the lead-time cost, or the slower response to a quality problem. A changeover on the *bottleneck* is lost throughput that can never be recovered, which is what makes this a throughput decision rather than a warehouse one.

### Operators are a shared resource the model has no state for

2 operators across 6 stations, each needing attention 35% of its cycle: **14.0% of attention demands go unmet**, costing about 4.9% of throughput.

The current model has no state for *waiting for a person* — a station can be up, unblocked and unstarved and still not running — so it counts that time as running. (binomial occupancy; crude, and the direction is the point.)

### Rework is the expensive failure, and only sometimes

First-pass yield 0.94, of which 3.6% is reworked and 2.4% scrapped. Loss: **2.3 parts/h (5.8%)**.

The rework loop re-enters at or before the constraint, so each reworked part consumes bottleneck capacity twice. Same defect rate, completely different consequence depending on where the loop closes — which is exactly what a line-level average hides.

## 2. Does the buffer recommendation survive the distribution family?

| cycle-time family | buffer 2 | buffer 5 | buffer 20 | gain 2→20 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| lognormal | 54.3 | 56.1 | 58.4 | **+4.1** |
| exponential | 44.4 | 51.7 | 58.3 | **+13.9** |
| constant | 54.7 | 56.0 | 58.4 | **+3.7** |

**The recommendation holds in all three families** — buffering helps whatever the cycle-time distribution — but the SIZE of the gain varies by 10.2 parts/h across them. So the direction is robust and the magnitude is a statement about my distributional choice, and **nobody measured the real one**. A business case built on the magnitude needs that measurement first.

## 3. Failures on busy time, not wall time

Wall-clock MTBF: **52.1 parts/h**. Utilisation-corrected: **56.7** (+8.7%).

A machine starved half the day does not accumulate wear while it sits there. Clocking failures on wall time gives an idle station the same failure rate as one running flat out, which understates the availability of lightly-loaded stations and misattributes failures to stations that were not working.

*first-order: MTBF scaled by utilisation. A proper implementation clocks the failure process only while the station is busy, which needs a change in the engine rather than in the spec.*

## 4. Validation as a gate

The README's item 3: Little's Law violations were counted and reported, not raised. **A check that cannot fail is documentation.** `python complete.py --gate  (exits non-zero on failure)`

| check | value | limit | passed | why it matters |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Little's Law (L = lambda W) | 0.005315 | 0.05 | **yes** | WIP, throughput and cycle time must be mutually consistent; if they are not, one of them is measured over the wrong window |
| throughput <= bottleneck effective capacity | 55.87 | 55.86 | **yes** | a line cannot beat its constraint; exceeding it means the constraint is mis-identified or the warm-up is being counted |
| conservation: created >= completed | 441 | 460 | **yes** | parts cannot be created by the simulation |
| station time fractions sum to <= 1 | 1 | 1 | **yes** | a station cannot be in two states at once |

Exit code 0 — 0 failed.

## 5. Animation and dashboard

`out/line.html`, 34 KB, self-contained, 240 frames of playback. The spec's red-flag list names "analysis without animation" and it is right for a reason that is not cosmetic: **trust in a simulation is built visually.** A plant manager who watches parts pile up in front of S3 and sees S4 starve believes the bottleneck result in a way no table achieves — and, more usefully, will spot a modelling error a table hides.
